deep.reconstruction:
Context (§76–78, Case III): water flows steadily from a vessel of cross-section ff and head AB = a through a horizontal tube BC of length b and cross-section gg, out of an orifice CC of area kk. In E260 Euler takes friction to be proportional to the local pressure, including the atmospheric pressure l, which he sets equal to a 30 ft water column. Friction therefore acts even at zero velocity. Along a channel of width f or g this gives exponential factors 𝔄 = e^{-αa/f} and 𝔅 = e^{-αb/g}. For a very wide vessel (𝔣 = k⁴/f⁴ ≈ 0) the steady-state head is v = [a𝔅(1−αa/2f) − (1−𝔅+(αa/f)𝔅) l] / [1−(1−𝔅)𝔤].

This page (§78 end – §81):
- Outflow requires v > 0, that is, e^{αb/g} < 1 + a/l − αa²/(2fl) − αa/f.
- Taking natural logarithms and expanding to first order in α gives αb/g < log(1+a/l) − αa(a+2l)/(2f(a+l)). Euler prints a+2f here.
- So flow stops when b > (g/α) log(1+a/l) − ag(a+2l)/(2f(a+l)).

§79 interpretation: the longer the horizontal tube, the slower the flow. Beyond a critical length no water comes out at all. Euler adds that this holds only if the orifice is at the top of the tube's end, because he neglected gravity inside the horizontal tube.

§80: for a ≪ l, log(1+a/l) ≈ a/l. The second term is small compared with the first (ratio of order αl/f), so the flow condition is b < g a/(α l).

§81: with a = 1 ft and l = 30 ft, flow stops when b > g/(30α). This gives a proposed experimental method for the friction constant: find the critical length b at which flow ceases, then α = g a/(b l). The next page (§§82–84) argues this beats capillary-tube methods, since capillaries have 'peculiar properties'. It gives a numerical example: g = 1/25 ft, b = 2 ft, α = 1/4000 gives threshold head a = 30/79 ft, and in general α = a/(50a+1500).

The mathematics is a one-dimensional steady balance with pressure-proportional (Coulomb/Amontons-type) wall friction. That law produces exponential pressure attenuation along a conduit and hence a static 'jamming' threshold.
errors: Algebraic slip repeated in §78, §79 and §80. From e^{αb/g} < 1 + a/l − αa²/(2fl) − αa/f, the first-order log gives a correction term αa(a+2l)/(2f(a+l)), not αa(a+2f)/(2f(a+l)). Hence the threshold should read b > (g/α)log(1+a/l) − ag(a+2l)/(2f(a+l)). This does not affect Euler's conclusions: he drops the term as small either way, since it is of relative order αl/f (corrected) or α (as printed).
The log step silently linearizes log(1+a/l − ε) ≈ log(1+a/l) − ε·l/(a+l). This is consistent with the first-order-in-α approximations already made for 𝔄 in §77.

Physical (not computational) defect: the existence of a finite critical length beyond which water cannot flow is an artifact of making friction proportional to absolute pressure, so that friction is nonzero at zero velocity. Real Newtonian liquids show no such threshold. Euler himself notes the model ignores gravity in the horizontal tube. The proposed experiment would in practice refute the friction law rather than measure α.

ideas.what: Wall friction of a fluid taken proportional to local pressure (including atmospheric pressure), giving exponential pressure attenuation e^{-αb/g} along a conduit
ideas.modern_name: Coulomb/Amontons-type friction applied to a continuum; mathematically the Janssen-type exponential law
ideas.usually_credited_to: Amontons (1699) for solids; Janssen (1895) for the exponential pressure law in granular columns
ideas.where_published: E260 itself (Novi Commentarii 6, 1756/57 [publ. 1761]); discussed in Truesdell's introduction to Opera omnia II.12 (unsure of the exact treatment)

ideas.what: Critical tube length (or critical head) beyond which steady outflow ceases: b_crit = (g/α)log(1+a/l) − O(α⁰ g a/f), approximately g a/(α l)
ideas.modern_name: Static friction threshold / plug jamming criterion (analogous to yield-stress onset of flow)
ideas.usually_credited_to: No standard credit in hydraulics, since the threshold is unphysical for water. Analogous criteria arise in granular plug flow and Bingham-plastic pipe flow (Bingham 1916).

ideas.what: Proposal to measure the friction coefficient α from the onset-of-flow threshold in a moderately wide horizontal tube, rather than from capillary flow rates
ideas.modern_name: Threshold (incipient-motion) measurement of a friction coefficient

ideas.what: First-order expansion log(1+a/l) ≈ a/l for small heads

missed.claim: Euler's pressure-proportional friction law produces exactly the exponential attenuation and log-type jamming criterion later central to granular mechanics: the Janssen silo law (1895) and the exponential force needed to push a frictional plug through a tube. Euler's 'no outflow if the tube is too long' is formally a granular-plug jamming length, b_crit ∝ (g/α) log(1 + driving pressure / ambient pressure). Euler's hydraulics is usually dismissed as wrong for water, and this structural kinship seems not to be remarked in the history of granular mechanics, though I am unsure.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical precedent for Janssen-type exponential wall-friction models and plug-jamming criteria. It is of interest mainly to historians of granular and frictional continuum mechanics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page derives a clean but physically spurious flow-stopping criterion from Euler's pressure-proportional friction, plus a small repeated algebra slip (a+2f should be a+2l). E260's friction law is known to Truesdell-era commentators. The formal Janssen/plug-jamming analogy may be unremarked but is of modest significance.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the printed text, including Euler's printed 'a+2f' in the numerators. That is an error in the original (it should be a+2l), not a transcription error.
In §81 the final formula is printed as α = (g/b)(a/l), i.e. α = g a/(b l); the transcription renders this correctly.
